description: We are a group of students who enjoy technology, solving problems, and learning new things. We come from a software engineering background and are excited to explore how technology can be used to tackle real-world challenges. We joined NASA Space Apps to challenge ourselves, work together, and turn our ideas into something meaningful.
summary:
We built MARSWALK, a tablet and helmet display that helps astronauts plan a safe walk on Mars. Think Google Maps for the first Marswalk, except it also knows the slope, the radiation, the dust and how much oxygen you have left.
Space suits are stiff and can’t handle slopes steeper than about 20°, and climbing burns oxygen fast. So instead of the shortest path, MARSWALK finds the safest one. It pulls together real NASA and USGS data from Mars orbiters and the Curiosity rover, including photos from the rover’s own camera. You can drag waypoints, swipe between map layers, watch oxygen, battery and radiation drop during the trip, and hit one button to get the safest route back to base. The controls are big enough to use with spacesuit gloves.
This matters because on Mars a wrong turn can cost lives. MARSWALK turns piles of planetary data into one simple answer: where can I safely walk, and how long can I stay out?
details:
What it does and how it works
MARSWALK shows astronauts a map of Gale Crater on Mars and plans a walking route that is safe for the suit. It reads ground slope from NASA elevation data and avoids anything steeper than 20°, the suit’s limit. Drag waypoints and the route updates instantly. Pick a safest route (gentle valleys) or a fastest one (least energy). Live gauges show oxygen, battery, body temperature and radiation dose, and one “Abort to Hab” button shows the shortest safe way home.

Benefits

  • Keeps astronauts off slopes the suit can’t handle
  • Shows how long oxygen will last before the walk
  • Puts photos, heat maps, minerals and elevation in one place
  • Works offline and with spacesuit gloves

Intended impact
Safer, easier planning of the first human walks on Mars, for astronauts and flight directors.

Tools and technology

  • React 18, TypeScript, Vite
  • MapLibre GL (2D), Three.js (3D)
  • Web Workers and A* routing
  • Data: NASA CTX, MOLA, THEMIS, CRISM, Curiosity Mastcam, REMS/RAD; USGS geologic map
  • Vitest (25/25 pass), offline PWA

What makes it creative
It treats the Marswalk as a navigation problem, not just a map. Real rover photos appear at each stop, a swipe slider compares layers, and a sun clock tracks the Martian day. Glove Mode and Zen Mode fit how astronauts work.

What we considered

  • The 20° slope limit
  • Energy and oxygen cost of climbing
  • Higher radiation on high ground
  • Real data only
  • Big buttons for gloves, no internet on Mars
